Goodman
GOOD-man
noun
From good + man, an old English title for the master of a household — the husband, the householder, the man who owns the house and answers for it. In the KJV it commonly stands in the phrase “the goodman of the house.”

Biblical Definition

The goodman is the master of the house — not a man who is morally good, but the householder, the head of the family, the owner who answers for what happens under his roof. Solomon uses it of the husband away on business: “the goodman is not at home, he is gone a long journey” (Pro 7:19), the adulteress’s excuse for her sin. In the parables it is the man who hires the labourers and against whom the murmurers grumble (Mat 20:11); in the upper room it is the householder to whom the disciples must say, “The Master saith, Where is the guestchamber?” (Mar 14:14). But the word’s weight falls on our Lord’s watchword: “if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up” (Mat 24:43; so Luk 12:39). Here is a doctrine of order and a doctrine of vigilance together. Christ assumes a man over the house, responsible for its keeping — the creational headship Scripture everywhere assumes, and which the church must not surrender. And He assumes that the hour is unknown. The whole point of the figure is that the goodman was not told which watch; had he known, he would have sat up. Because he does not know, he must watch always. Every Christian householder is a goodman under the great Householder, keeping his house against a coming he cannot date and must not miss.

Webster 1828 Definition

The master of a house; the householder, the head of a family; not one who is morally good but the man who owns and answers for the house.

GOODMAN, the master of a house or family; a householder; the husband.

From good and man, an old title of the head of a household.

It does not mean a man of good morals but the owner of the house.

The goodman is not at home, he is gone a long journey (Pro 7:19).

Christ’s watchword: the goodman knew not in what watch the thief would come (Mat 24:43).

Key Scripture

Mat 20:11 — "And when they had received it, they murmured against the goodman of the house,"

Mat 24:43 — "But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up."

Mar 14:14 — "And wheresoever he shall go in, say ye to the goodman of the house, The Master saith, Where is the guestchamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples?"

Luk 12:39 — "And this know, that if the goodman of the house had known what hour the thief would come, he would have watched, and not have suffered his house to be broken through."

Modern Corruption

A live misuse: the watchfulness Christ commands is traded for date-setting, which is the very thing the figure forbids — the goodman was not told the watch.

expand to see more

Here is a live misuse, and it is worth naming plainly. Our Lord’s figure of the goodman turns wholly on ignorance of the hour: if he had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched. He did not know. Therefore he must watch always. Yet the popular prophecy industry of the last two centuries has done the opposite with the very text — charting the watch, dating the coming, printing the year, and calling that watchfulness. It is not. It is the goodman deciding he knows the hour and going to bed for the other three watches. The date-setting habit is a fruit of the dispensational system Darby and Scofield bequeathed to the modern church, a scheme unknown to any Reformation confession; and every failed date it has produced has made the world laugh at the blessed hope. Christ did not give a timetable. He gave a charge: watch, for ye know neither the day nor the hour.

The word also guards an order the age would like to dissolve. The goodman of the house is the man of the house, the householder responsible for its keeping, and Christ frames His parable on that assumption as on solid ground — as Scripture does everywhere, setting the husband as head of the wife and the father as the one who answers for his household before God. To sneer at the very notion of a man over a house is to quarrel not with an old English word but with the creational order the Lord Himself takes for granted. Recover both halves: let the Christian man own his charge as the goodman under the great Householder, and let him keep his house awake, for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the master of a house, the householder who owns and answers for it.

expand to see more

Goodman — from good + man, an old title of the householder.

It denotes the master of the house, the husband, the head of the family.

It carries no sense of moral goodness; it names an office, not a character.

In the parables it is the householder who hires, owns, and answers (Mat 20:11).

Christ makes him the figure of the watchful saint who knows not the hour (Mat 24:43).

Usage

"The goodman of the house is the master of it — the office, not a verdict on his morals."

"Had the goodman known the watch, he would have watched: he was not told, so he watches always."

"Say ye to the goodman of the house, The Master saith — even the upper room was asked of its head."
